valley.drawingAlt: Reeds at dusk. A flock of starlings rises from the water, and the reflection shows more birds than the sky.
locals: The flock goes up when enough of us go up. Not before.
The water shows more birds in the sky than there are. Do not believe the water.
Tove has never left the reeds. Tove says the reeds are enough.

notes.title: Enough neighbors
notes.science: Some things spread only when several neighbors do them first. One bird lifting off is not enough to lift the flock.
notes.limits: Each starling here counts only its seven nearest birds. Real starlings track about that many, and they also see the shape of the whole flock.
notes.counter: Some ideas spread from one friend alone.
notes.question: What would you do only once enough friends did it?

sources.label: Interaction Ruling Animal Collective Behavior, Ballerini and others, 2008
The Spread of Behavior in an Online Social Network Experiment, Centola, 2010

notes.title: The majority illusion
notes.science: When the best-known birds fly, it can look as if most birds fly. The birds with the most ties are seen by the most others.
notes.limits: The water's picture here uses one simple weighting.
notes.counter: Often what looks common is common.
notes.question: Who do you see most, and are they like everyone else?

sources.label: The Majority Illusion in Social Networks, Lerman, Yan and Wu, 2016
Why Your Friends Have More Friends Than You Do, Feld, 1991
